# Automation of Incidents in Practice: AWS DevOps Agent & Amazon CloudWatch

The video shows how to get out of the manual incident investigation for an automatic flow with AWS DevOps Agent and Amazon CloudWatch. It goes through tags that allow you to map the topology, a CPU alarm, an Agent Spaces isolation, and an example where the agent reads the support call, finds the root cause, and proposes a mitigation plan.

Video by Maurício Yokoyama Issei, published on May 5, 2026 (8 min 39 s).
Watch: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f8xd4FOBYfU

_The video and the transcript are in Portuguese. The minutes between brackets, such as [04:12], point to the excerpt of the video._

## The problem: putting out fire

Video is a tutorial for infrastructure operations teams. The proposal is to exchange the solution of reactive problems with a proactive and automated flow with AWS tools [00:00].

"The site is slow" is the phrase that scares the most who works in operations. Such a complaint usually opens hours of manual investigation, with fragmented telemetry and log jumps in log [00:20].

On the one hand, the manual process: the time to detect and resolve grows, the metrics are scattered and the friction between teams is inevitable [00:41]. On the other hand, the support connected directly to an automatic diagnosis with AWS DevOps Agent. According to the video, resolution time drops from hours to minutes [01:02].

## The Cost of Manual Investigation

Structural failure is classic. Support is in the front line, but it lacks deep knowledge of infrastructure to diagnose complex causes [01:44].

DevOps engineers are supposed to build improvements, but they're pulled to put out fires. This goes and comes generates friction and a cycle of only reactive solutions [02:04].

## Tags: the basis of automation

The basis for automating is an organized infrastructure with good tag practices [02:26]. Tags are metadata labels, with an optional key and value, which classify each feature by purpose, team or environment [02:26].

Without tags, the AI tool is almost blind. It is with them that DevOps Agent maps the relations between the parts of the application during an investigation [02:46]. The AWS article treats tags as optional, but recommends using them to focus on the application components.

A tag strategy goes beyond cost allocation. It covers access control, operations and support, and accelerates incident management and automatic updates [03:09].

## Proactive Monitoring with CloudWatch

With metadata ready, the next step is observability. Amazon CloudWatch collects telemetry in real time [03:29].

The paradigm shift: instead of waiting for support to open a call, the team receives the degradation alert before the end user feels the problem [03:51]. CloudWatch tracks metrics, mounts panels, sends limit alerts and triggers automatic responses [04:12].

## A three-step CPU alarm

The video shows a CPU alarm in three steps [04:12]:

1. Choose the metric, such as using the CPU of the EC2 instance running the database [04:32].
2. Set a static limit. In the example, CPU above 85% for more than 5 minutes [04:32].
3. Configure the action: scale the environment or send a notification to Amazon EventBridge, which can start the DevOps Agent investigation [04:53].

## Isolation with Agent Spaces

Giving the agent autonomy requires control. An Agent Space functions as a clean laboratory room: a logical container that defines which AWS accounts, tools and parts of the infrastructure the agent can access [05:14].

The video recommends creating multiple Agent Spaces to separate development production, separate teams, limit services or meet compliance requirements [05:35].

The isolation has several layers: the AWS account, the users who can talk to the agent and the investigation data, including the conversation history [05:56]. What happens in an Agent Space stays in it [06:17].

## The autonomous resolution in practice

The prerequisites of the example are Agentforce Service with a configured MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that bridges with Salesforce; an Agent Space; CloudWatch and AWS CloudTrail; and infrastructure with tags [06:37].

With this, the agent reads the support calls and searches the infrastructure data [06:58]. The flow of the example [06:58]:

1. A customer opens a call saying that the application has fallen, and the flow fires itself [06:58].
2. DevOps Agent retrieves the details of the case and, by tags, discovers the application topology [06:58].
3. He analyzes the CloudWatch metrics and sees that the requests have fallen to zero [07:19].
4. It crosses this with CloudTrail events and reaches the root cause: someone closed the instance EC2 by mistake [07:19].

The agent not only finds the cause: he publishes the technical context in the call and generates a mitigation plan, with step-by-step instructions and architectural recommendations to avoid repetition [07:39].

## What's left for the team

The video closes with a question: if the manual search for logs is automated, how will the team use the time? The proposed response is to focus on resilience and real improvements [08:00]. According to the video, automation does not replace talent: it releases it [08:20].

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What are the tags for in the DevOps Agent investigation?

They let the agent map the relationships between the application resources and investigate only what matters [02:46].

### Why create more than one Agent Space?

To separate development production, separate teams and meet compliance requirements without one research seeing data from another [05:35].

## About the video

Do you still waste hours investigating infrastructure incidents, crossing logs from different services and climbing problems manually? AWS DevOps Agent has arrived to change this scenario and reduce its resolution time (MTTR) from hours to minutes!
In this infrastructure operations team-focused tutorial (Cloud Ops and SRE), we will perform a practical deep dive and demonstrate how to create an autonomous monitoring and response flow to end-to-end incidents.
What you will learn in this video: • Essential Configuration: How to enable and connect AWS DevOps Agent to Amazon CloudWatch to adopt a proactive response posture
. • CPU Alarms in Practice: Demonstration of how to set up an Alarm in CloudWatch based CPU metrics to trigger research triggers immediately
. • Environmental isolation (Agent Spaces): Learn to use multiple "DevOps Agent Spaces" to safely separate production and non-production environments investigations, ensuring access isolation (IAM), integrated tools and data
. • Good Tag Practice (Tagging): Find out how the correct application of AWS resources tags is the secret to allowing the Agent to do the "Dynamic Topology Mapping", ensuring that he investigates only the relevant components of your application during a crisis
.
In addition, we discuss how this architecture connects with Salesforce Hosted MCP Server to create autonomous mitigation plans that go directly to customer support calls, ending friction between service and engineering teams
.
Official Links and Reference Materials (Documentation):
